A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TF-Restormer with the same title, authors and underlying research. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison.

before.justification: v3 reports original restoration, denoising, super-resolution and streaming results, alongside architecture, loss and sampling-rate ablations.

after.justification: v4 retains those empirical results and adds real-recording and REVERB evaluations, spectral-error statistics and an URGENT loss-control experiment.

M1.justification: The encoder–decoder, extension queries, conditional cross-attention, frequency projections, Mamba streaming variant and training losses are retained. The xSFI terminology and expanded band-partitioned attention description clarify the existing procedure. The additional URGENT variant tests an existing loss configuration.

E1.justification: v4 adds DNS 2020 real recordings, REVERB real recordings, REVERB-Sim and a combined REVERB-DNS noise condition (Table 4c–d; Appendix M). These substantially broaden evaluation environments. The existing DNS synthetic evaluations and renamed VCTK noisy-distorted data are retained.

E2.justification: New comparisons include Miipher and Resemble-Enhance on DNS real recordings, and WPE, WRN, GCRN, TCN+SA, D-MFMVDR, DCN and TF-GridNet in the REVERB evaluations. Table 18 explicitly imports published baseline scores. Comparator sets in the retained experiments remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Appendix M introduces dereverberation metrics including CD, LLR, SNRfw and SRMR, near/far averaging, and a −10 to 0 dB added-noise protocol with retrained discriminative baselines. Appendix J adds an URGENT control using the original loss configuration. Existing training budgets, splits and benchmark protocols are retained.

E4.justification: v4 adds empirical magnitude–error and normalization analyses (Figure 4; Table 13), an URGENT control testing the explanation for the perceptual–fidelity trade-off (Table 14), and added-noise robustness evaluation on REVERB-DNS (Table 20). Existing architecture, spectral-loss and sampling-distribution ablations are retained.

E5.justification: Table 13 newly reports Spearman correlations, coefficients of variation and significance summarized as all p≈0. This adds statistical analysis without introducing multi-seed performance estimates, confidence intervals or documented increases in repeated runs.

E6.justification: Substantial new results include REVERB-Sim PESQ/SRMR of 2.825/8.004, REVERB-DNS results of 2.113/8.586, and URGENT original-loss control PESQ/UTMOS of 1.82/3.08. Real-recording scores and correlation findings are also added. Retained result rows match, apart from equivalent rounding in Table 6.

T1.justification: Beyond v3's proposed-loss gradient discussion, v4 introduces three formal loss-design criteria and a robust-loss comparison with derivatives, peak heights and normalization derivations (Appendix H; Table 12). The added mathematics contains an error: the displayed normalized Geman–McClure loss has peak gradient 1/w², contradicting the claimed unit peak.

C1.justification: The four central contributions retain the same decoupled-rate architecture, shared SFI discriminator, frequency projection and streaming support, and scaled spectral loss. Naming the setting xSFI and adding supporting evaluations do not materially change these core claims.

C2.justification: v4 develops a heteroscedasticity-based interpretation of adaptive loss scaling, attributes the URGENT trade-off more specifically to loss rebalancing, and explicitly frames transfer comparisons as OOD evidence. Appendix N newly acknowledges the missing subjective listening study; existing hallucination, language and multi-speaker limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix N newly identifies a public implementation and pretrained-weight repository, beyond v3's anonymous code/demo disclosure. Frequency-grid and projection-sharing details are clarified. Conversely, v4 omits v3's explicit pretraining objective Lpre=100Lp+Ls while still referring to Lpre. Hardware, optimizer and model configurations remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v4 adds REVERB/dereverberation references and cites Quan and Li (2024b) for streaming design and Shin and Park (2026) for TF architectures, while retaining the broader positioning. A new attribution is inconsistent: Table 18 cites Wang et al. (2017) for TCN+SA, but that bibliography entry concerns image segmentation.

P1.justification: The abstract, introductory motivation, encoder–decoder explanation, loss rationale and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting. xSFI terminology is introduced throughout, appendix material is split and reordered, and limitations are reorganized into topical paragraphs. These changes extend beyond inserting new experimental content.

P2.justification: v4 adds a detailed architecture diagram, redraws the module figure into three panels, expands the gradient visualization with a logarithmic axis, and adds error-distribution and loss-family plots. Table 4 expands from two to four panels, with additional analytical and REVERB tables and extensive relocation of retained displays.

improvement.justification: The added REVERB transfer tests and URGENT loss control strengthen empirical support and test a previously asserted explanation; the listening-study limitation also improves qualification of perceptual claims. These gains outweigh localized problems, but the faulty normalization in Table 12, mismatched baseline citation in Table 18 and less explicit pretraining objective limit the overall improvement.
